short: Published in 438 CE, the Codex Theodosianus was the first official compilation of imperial law since Constantine, and shaped codes for centuries.
full:
On 15 February 438, Theodosius II published the Codex Theodosianus, a compilation begun by an imperial commission in 429 that gathered and abridged every general imperial constitution issued since 312. Organised into sixteen books by subject, from religion to taxation to the courts, it replaced a scattered mass of individual edicts with a single authoritative reference and was adopted in the western empire the same year under Valentinian III.

The Code gave later jurists a single starting point instead of scattered archives, and it influenced barbarian law codes issued in former Roman territory after 476, including the Breviary of Alaric. It was eventually superseded in the east by Justinian's more extensive Codex Justinianus in 529, but for nearly a century it stood as the definitive statement of Roman law.
